Author: anfroholic
Content:
I do remember asking that. This is a neat compilation, but does seem moore's law-esque, which I don't think answers my question in the spirit of the way I meant it. 

I think a refined version sounds like:
What *[novel and useful]* things will people do with *[trailing edge]* silicon. 

Admittedly the ignorance I had *(and still have)* didn't allow me to comprehend the landscape, let alone understand what the possibilities or challenges really are. 

Now we're starting to see extra flashy things like [microTheia](https://github.com/dhgaddy/microTheia) and I always love novel architectures like @BreakingTaps. As I learn about the sweet spot for gf180mcu I am super excited to see what comes from @Tim Edwards Chipalooza, and more to the point; things people will do with those analog blocks, and I literally have given talks about many of the other awesome ones *[coming soon I hope]*.

So, I'll never stop asking "What will people do with silicon?", but will say I'm honored to be a part of this with you all, and thank you for everything you've shared with me and with us all! 
And can't wait to see what you all come up with next!

-# p.s. I can't really see myself being interested in any press release broadcom will ever make again ;)

I think there is some interesting things there -- like the mm2 went up despite the process node going down, the different revisions on the same process node, & the fact that RPi -- which isn't that of a small customer only went with custom silicon as a last resort despite having 1/3rd of their silicon take up by stuff they didn't use.

I wonder what the world looks like if their second / third design used custom silicon.....

Content: My current ***theory*** is that as the cost to make the cheap went up (because they are using a more advanced process node) they needed to cramp more stuff into the chip to justify the expense -- so even though the node has a lot more transistors per mm2 they end up using more mm2 in total.
